verdicts.claim: Manpower-supply empanelment at a bank subsidiary requires Rs 25 crore turnover, Rs 1 crore average PAT, 3 years and 1,000 placements
verdicts.issue: Verified verbatim in the PNB Cards & Services RFP (downloaded and extracted). Confirmed exactly: in the manpower-services business for banks/FIs/insurers/PSUs/MNCs/large corporates 'for at least 3 years'; 'An annual gross turnover of at least Rs.25 crores in any of one year within last 3 years'; 'average net profit after tax of at least Rs. 1.00 crore for the last 03 audited financial years viz. 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25'; 'should have supplied manpower of minimum no. of 1,000' to banks/FIs/insurers/PSUs; multi-state presence evidenced by GST certificates of different states; 'a certified copy of License from Labour Commissioner to employ Contract Labour under Contract Labour Act'; no blacklisting by any Public Sector Bank, RBI, IBA or other government agency. On canvassing the document reads 'the same will be mount to disqualification' (sic) — the claim's paraphrase 'will amount to disqualification' corrects an original typo. The conclusion that a pre-revenue vendor cannot clear these gates is correct.

verdicts.claim: IT-services empanelment gates require ~Rs 10 crore average turnover, three years positive net worth and 12 certified staff held three years
verdicts.issue: Verified in the IDBI RFP eligibility compliance sheet: turnover gate stated as 'Rs.10 crore (Rs.5 crore for MSE) towards Information Technology Service' over the past three financial years; 'Bidder should have positive Net Worth' in the past three financial years; minimum three years in the ITSP business; a pool of 'full time minimum 12 professionals' holding listed certifications; and the blacklisting bar covering government bodies, PSBs and PSUs 'during the last five years'. The referenced financial years in the document are FY2019-20 to FY2021-22, consistent with the 29 June 2022 issue date. The claim's observation that these gates are lower than the manpower-supply gates at PNBCSL is borne out by direct comparison (Rs 10 crore turnover and no PAT requirement, versus Rs 25 crore turnover plus Rs 1 crore average PAT plus 1,000 placements).

verdicts.claim: Some empanelments impose a hard 10-year-existence gate plus three years of EBITDA profit and minimum permanent headcount
verdicts.issue: Verified in the Union Bank RFP pre-qualification criteria. Confirmed: the bidder 'should be in existence for last 10 years as on' the cut-off date; 'minimum annual turnover of Rs.8 Crores during the last three financial years' with the explicit restriction that 'It should be individual company turnover and not that of any group of companies'; 'The bidder should have positive operating profit (EBITDA i.e. Earnings before Interest...)' in the last three financial years; 'The bidder should have mandatorily minimum 30 permanent employees as on' the cut-off, of which five must hold CISA/CISM/CISSP; and Earnest Money Deposit of 'Rs. 4,00,000/- (Rs Four Lakhs Only)'. The Mumbai-and-Hyderabad presence requirement was not individually located in the extracted text, though the RFP is issued from the CISO Office in Hyderabad. The claim's own caveat — that the scope is IT/cyber-security services rather than pure staffing, but the shape of the gate is representative — is appropriately hedged.

verdicts.claim: MSME and DPIIT-startup registration is the one documented concession that materially lowers these barriers
verdicts.issue: Verified in both documents, and this is the most actionable positive finding in the procurement block. IDBI sets the turnover gate at 'Rs.10 crore (Rs.5 crore for MSE)' — a genuine halving. Union Bank states verbatim: 'In case of bidders registered with NSIC/Udyog Aadhaar as MSME or a Start-up Company, they are eligible for waiver of EMD', with MSEs providing a valid NSIC certificate under the single point registration scheme or Udyog Aadhaar, and start-ups 'required to submit Certificate of Recognition issued by Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce & Industry, Government of India', plus a Chartered Accountant-signed Annexure R. The EMD at stake is Rs 4,00,000. The caveat that the MSE must still meet all other criteria is correct and important — the concession lowers two gates, not the experience and headcount gates that actually exclude a new entrant. The 2012 policy order and 2018 amendment citations were not separately verified.

verdicts.claim: Enterprise requisitions set a relevant-and-current experience floor of ~4+ years, excluding freshers entirely
verdicts.issue: Verified in the SBI RFP's role specifications, which state '4 + Years' relevant and current experience (with other role lines showing '4+ years exp' and '4+ years experience'), alongside the degree requirements and the footnote verbatim: 'The previous experience letter should explicitly mention the nature of duties performed by the resource.' The training-cost allocation is also confirmed verbatim: where training is required to upskill the resources, 'the same shall be taken up by the Service Provider and no cost shall be borne by the Bank for the same.' The RFP adds that the Bank will not bear candidate travel or visit charges either. The conclusion that freshers are excluded from these requisition line items follows directly, and the experience-letter-of-duties requirement makes a trained-but-unplaced bench structurally unevidenceable for these roles — the sharpest single constraint in the set.

verdicts.claim: The client controls selection and replacement economics; substitution terms are punitive and make a thin bench a liability
verdicts.issue: Most of this is verified verbatim in the SBI RFP, but one clause is misdescribed. Confirmed: 'the decision of Bank to onboard the resource will be final and binding on the Service Provider'; 'The Bank will not consider substitution/replacement of any resources prior to completion of 3 months from the date of joining'; 'In case the resource is not found satisfactory within 15 (fifteen) days of joining, the Bank may ask for replacement of such resource and no payment shall be made for the period'; on attrition, 'a notice period of 45 (forty-five) days along with CVs of a minimum 200%... of total number of resource(s) to be substituted', '(Substitution for a resource is allowed maximum up to 2 times)', knowledge transfer 'for at least a month', and 'The Bank will not make payment for the substitution resource during transition and knowledge transfer period'; and absence without prior approval penalised at 'twice the rate per hour per resource'. Wrong: there is no 3-working-day CV replacement clause. The RFP requires CVs for at least 200% of the resources required within 7 working days of PO acceptance, with liquidated damages of 0.01% of PO value per day capped at 0.5%; separately, a 10%-of-PO-value LD and possible termination (with award to L-2) arise where fewer than 70% of shortlisted resources report within 15 days.
verdicts.corrected: SBI terms: the bank interviews every resource and 'the decision of Bank to onboard the resource will be final and binding on the Service Provider'; CVs for at least 200% of the resources required must be supplied within 7 working days of PO acceptance, with liquidated damages per day of delay; at least 70% of shortlisted resources must report within 15 days of result intimation, failing which the bank may terminate and award to L-2; if unsatisfactory within 15 days of joining the bank may demand replacement and 'no payment shall be made for the period'; no substitution in the first 3 months; on attrition, 45 days' notice plus 'CVs of a minimum 200%... of total number of resource(s) to be substituted', maximum 2 substitutions per role, at least one month of knowledge transfer, and 'The Bank will not make payment for the substitution resource during transition and knowledge transfer period.' Absence without approval is penalised at twice the hourly rate.

verdicts.claim: Background and police verification are contractual deliverables with 7-day and 90-day clocks, and subcontracting is prohibited
verdicts.issue: Verified verbatim in the SBI RFP: 'Service Provider will submit BGC (Background Check) as per the prescribed format of the Bank and PVR (Police Verification Report) applied for copy within 7 (seven) days of boarding of resources. Police Verification Report duly issued by Police authorities shall be submitted within 90 (ninety) days of onboarding of resource.' Biometrics confirmed: 'Biometrics of resources will be captured at the time of onboarding for the purpose of attendance.' Subcontracting confirmed twice: 'As per the scope of this RFP, sub-contracting is not permitted' in the RFP body and again in the draft agreement, reinforced by the Appendix-E line 'Third-Party Components: Not Applicable (No Outsourcing allowed)'. The Gujarat Informatics consortium bar ('Any kind of consortium will not be allowed') was not verified, as I did not reach that tender; the Union Bank consortium bar was likewise not located.

verdicts.claim: The cash-flow structure is pay-first bill-later, with payment conditional on proof of statutory remittances
verdicts.issue: The Gujarat Informatics tender was not reachable, so its specific clauses — 20-day payment on bill submission, the conditionality on PF/professional tax/ESIC challans for the previous month, and 'the agency will have to make payment to the manpower provided within 7 days from the end of the month irrespective of the pending payment from GIL' — are unconfirmed, and they carry the claim. Two supporting elements are verified: the SBI RFP confirms payment 'not exceeding 30 (thirty) days after its receipt thereof' of the invoice, and the Quess Q1 FY27 deck confirms 'GS DSO days at 28' with AR stable (the Q4 FY26 deck shows Average AR DSO of 15 days and Collect & Pay at 76%). Note those Quess figures are general-staffing metrics, which the Frost & Sullivan finding establishes do not apply to an IT-staffing book — so they support the thesis only indirectly.

verdicts.claim: Insurance cover is an onboarding requirement with a defined floor, evidenced on demand
verdicts.issue: Verified in the IDBI RFP clause 45. Confirmed: 'Third party motor vehicle liability insurance as required under Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 in respect of motor vehicles operated in India by the Bidder or their personnel for the period of the Contract'; 'Third party liability insurance with a sufficient coverage for the period of the Contract'; 'Professional liability insurance, with a minimum coverage equal to estimated remuneration and reimbursable'; and 'Employer's liability and workers' compensation insurance in respect of the personnel of the Bidder, in accordance with the relevant provisions of the applicable law, as well as, with respect to such personnel, any such life, health, accident, travel or other insurance as may be appropriate'. The clause also requires insurance against loss or damage to equipment, the bidder's property used in performing the services, and documents prepared — a further obligation the claim omits. The 'take out and maintain at their own cost' and evidence-on-request wording sits at the head of the same clause.

verdicts.claim: The buying centre differs by what is bought — HR owns off-roll manpower, IT vendor-management owns IT services, the CISO owns security
verdicts.issue: Verified across the three tender documents. PNB Cards & Services names the 'Chief People Officer' as Empanelment/RFP Coordinator for off-roll manpower supply, and all correspondence is addressed to that office. IDBI's empanelment carries the reference IDBI-Bank/ITD/VMG/RFP/22-23/21, i.e. IT Department / Vendor Management Group, as claimed. Union Bank's ITCSSP empanelment is issued from its CISO Office in Hyderabad (the document's header and scope confirm the cyber-security framing; the exact office string was partially legible in extraction). The SBI RFP is an IT procurement with a mandatory business-unit interview of every resource. The conclusion that there is no single door into an enterprise is well supported and is a genuinely useful go-to-market insight. The specific contact email addresses were present in the PNBCSL document.

verdicts.claim: Verifiable RFP-to-revenue windows at large Indian buyers run roughly 2 to 5 months from publication to contract start
verdicts.issue: Verified against the three documents. SBI: RFP dated 1 November 2025 for a contract commencing 1 January 2026 — two months — with shortlisted resources required to report within 15 days of result intimation. PNBCSL: queries due 8 December 2025 (consistent with a 2 December 2025 issue), bid validity stated as 90 days from the last date of submission in the schedule table, and empanelment effective FY2026-27, i.e. from 1 April 2026 — about four months. Union Bank: RFP of November 2024 with criteria as on 30.09.2024, empanelment effective 01.04.2025 — about five months. The claim's crucial qualifier is correct and well made: these are the clocks for an already-qualified bidder, and a vendor that must first become empanelled adds the full EOI cycle plus the wait to the next window, which the five-year IDBI and three-year PNBCSL terms show can be years.

verdicts.claim: The Government e-Marketplace is a lower-barrier channel producing the dated purchase orders enterprise scoring matrices reward
verdicts.issue: Verified on gem.gov.in directly. Confirmed: 350 service categories and 10,671 product categories; cumulative order value displayed as 2,131,529 crore (Rs 21,31,529 crore); dedicated manpower categories including 'Manpower Outsourcing Services - Minimum wage' and 'Manpower Outsourcing Services - Fixed Remuneration', plus security manpower services; and seller self-registration at mkp.gem.gov.in. The strategic inference is the valuable part and it is sound: because Union Bank's matrix awards one mark per BFSI purchase order in India and two per global PO, and IDBI and PNBCSL both require documentary work orders, GeM orders convert directly into future empanelment eligibility points. This is the one route in the set that a pre-revenue vendor can actually take today.

verdicts.claim: GCCs account for 71% of Quess professional-staffing headcount and 68% of segment revenue
verdicts.issue: Duplicate of an earlier finding; verified verbatim in the Quess Q1 FY27 deck. 'GCC contributing 71% of headcount with 68% of revenue contribution'; segment headcount 7,129 with 'growth of 7% YoY'; revenue Rs 252 cr; EBITDA Rs 28 cr at 11.0% margin against 12.8% in Q4 FY26; 'Added 36 contracts during the quarter'; 'Open mandates at 1,100+ primarily in niche and high value roles'. Client concentration for Q1 FY27 confirmed from the chart as Top 10% = 40%, Next 40% = 50%, Others = 10%. One note for the write-up: the client-concentration series shows the top decile of clients falling from 46% of revenue in Q1'26 to 40% in Q1'27 while 'Others' rose from 19% to 20-25%, so concentration is easing slightly — context the claim omits.

verdicts.claim: Serving GCC demand needs a 450-recruiter, 300-client, 80-city engine at ~Rs 1.18 lakh monthly billing per associate on ~22% gross margin
verdicts.issue: Verified in the Quess Q1 FY27 deck. The Quess IT Staffing & Solutions slide states verbatim 'delivering skilled IT talent and managed technology solutions to 300+ enterprises across 80+ cities', with '~7,000 Associates deployed', '800+ Technology skill domains', '450+ Specialist IT recruiters' and '30K+ Monthly talent outreach'. The group-level slide confirms 'Recruiters: 700+' and ~482,000 active associates. The unit economics check out exactly: Rs 252 cr over 7,129 associates = Rs 3.53 lakh per associate per quarter = Rs 1.18 lakh per month; and 'Gross margin to EBITDA margin conversion remains above 50%' on an 11.0% EBITDA margin implies roughly 20-22% gross margin. Group EBITDA margin of 2.02% in Q1 FY27 is also confirmed on the highlights slide.

verdicts.claim: IT staffing is the slowest-growing part of a flat Indian staffing market — 2% QoQ against 2.6% for general staffing
verdicts.issue: The core comparison is confirmed on the ISF research page for Q1 2026-27: overall industry growth 7.5% YoY, formal flexi workforce 1.95 million, 1.14 lakh new formal flexi jobs over 12 months, and quarter-over-quarter growth of 2.6% in General Staffing against 2% in IT Staffing (with IT at 7% YoY). This is a useful and under-appreciated datapoint, since it reverses the widely repeated 'IT staffing is the fastest-growing segment' line from FY26. Not confirmed: ISF's forward projection of a ~9.16 million flexi workforce by FY27 from 7.2 million in FY25 — no such projection appears on the page, and those magnitudes are an order above the 1.95 million ISF-member figure, so they likely refer to a different (whole-market) basis and should not be mixed with the member series.
verdicts.corrected: Indian Staffing Federation, Q1 2026-27: overall staffing industry grew 7.5% year-over-year; ISF members represent a formal flexi workforce of 1.95 million; 1.14 lakh new formal flexi jobs added over 12 months; quarter-over-quarter growth was 2.6% in General Staffing against 2% in IT Staffing (IT at 7% YoY). The ~9.16 million FY27 projection is not published on the ISF research page and is unverified.

verdicts.claim: Hyderabad accounts for 40% of all new GCC setups in India, against India hosting 1,700 of the world's 3,200 GCCs
verdicts.issue: The NASSCOM Voices page returned HTTP 406 Not Acceptable and I could not retrieve it, so none of the figures is confirmed: 1,700 of 3,200 centres globally, 60% leading product development or deep analytics, Hyderabad at 40% of new GCC setups, tier-2 cities at 21% YoY hiring growth, 120,000+ AI/ML professionals, 185+ AI/ML COEs, or the 2%-of-GDP and 2.8-million-jobs 2030 projections. Two cautions regardless of verification: the claim's own description identifies this as a NASSCOM Voices community contribution carrying a disclaimer, so it is an authored opinion piece hosted by NASSCOM rather than NASSCOM research; and its 1,700-GCC and 120,000-AI-professional figures conflict with the verified NASSCOM-Zinnov release (2,117 GCCs, ~250,000 AI professionals), so the two should not be cited together.

verdicts.claim: The dominant competitor to a train-and-deploy vendor is the GCC's own internal reskilling, reported as 2.5x cheaper
verdicts.issue: Same unreachable source (HTTP 406), so the 78% of GCCs reskilling internal teams for GenAI, the 2.5x cost advantage of upskilling over external hiring, the 60%-longer retention for high-internal-mobility employees, the 120% growth in AI talent concentration 2019-2025, the 4.7x global AI literacy multiple and the '6% or fewer' applied-skills figure are all unconfirmed — and the 2.5x figure is the one that matters, since it is the direct price argument against Anvi's offer. Note the verified Taggd survey cuts the other way on the headline: it puts internal development at 22% of GCC talent acquisition against 78% external, which is hard to square with '78% of GCCs are already reskilling' being the dominant mode. Resolve this before it shapes positioning; as it stands the reskilling-substitution thesis rests on an opinion piece I could not read.

verdicts.claim: The Labour Codes came into force 21 November 2025 with central rules notified May 2026, and the cost impact is material at scale
verdicts.issue: Two of three elements verified, from better sources than the one cited. The in-force date is confirmed in the Cyril Amarchand guide, which records the operative act: 'On November 21, 2025, by notifications issued by the Ministry of Labour and Employment' the Codes came into force (the guide also notes a corrigendum of 19 December 2025 modifying the 21 November notification, and transition relief running to 21 November 2026 — useful detail the claim omits). The Quess cost impact is confirmed verbatim in the Q1 FY27 deck: 'One time Revenue increase impact of Rs 176 Cr, during the quarter due to new Labor Code'. Not verified: the 'central rules notified in May 2026' and phased state-level implementation, which rest on a Mondaq law-firm article I did not reach — and that is a government-notification claim, so it needs the Ministry of Labour and Employment or the Gazette, not trade commentary.
verdicts.corrected: The Labour Codes came into force on 21 November 2025 by notifications of the Ministry of Labour and Employment (with a corrigendum of 19 December 2025 and transition relief to 21 November 2026), while State-level implementation continues in phases. Quess Corp's Q1 FY27 General Staffing commentary records a 'One time Revenue increase impact of Rs 176 Cr, during the quarter due to new Labor Code', confirming a quantified billing/cost effect on staffing vendors. The May 2026 central-rules notification date is unverified and should be confirmed against the Gazette.

verdicts.claim: GCC legal and HR gate staffing vendors on co-employment risk, requiring compliance obligations, indemnities, audit rights and visible separation
verdicts.issue: I did not reach the Mondaq article, so the specific guidance — that vendor contracts should 'contain labour-law compliance obligations, indemnities, audit rights and access-control obligations', that the GCC must 'maintain a clear distinction between vendor employees and GCC employees in reporting lines, email domains, system access and HR processes', the disguised-employment risk factors, and that 'payment for work does not automatically mean ownership of IP' — is unconfirmed as quoted. The substance is strongly corroborated by sources I did verify: the CAM guide establishes that the OSH Code makes welfare obligations the principal employer's primary responsibility and attaches liability where the contractor is unlicensed, and expressly excludes personnel 'regularly employed by, and are paid wages and provided benefits by, the contractor' from 'contract labour' — which is precisely why buyer legal teams interrogate payroll and licence status. So the operational conclusion stands on verified ground even though this source does not.

verdicts.claim: NASSCOM/NSDL National Skills Registry: 337 subscriber companies, 37,22,697 web registrations, 25,86,677 ITPINs, 25 empanelled background checkers
verdicts.issue: All four counters match the live page exactly, as does the 'List of Empanelled Background Checkers' link. No as-of date is printed, as the finding correctly concedes — so the figures are undateable and cannot be used to show a trend.

verdicts.claim: GCC contract roles rising 1 in 5 → 1 in 4 → 1 in 3 by FY27
verdicts.issue: The page carries the wording, but the sourcing chain is weaker than the finding states. The 1-in-5/1-in-4/1-in-3 progression is footnoted to a 2024 Staffing Industry article, NOT to Quess's Q4 FY26 GCC Trends Report; Quess is cited only for the C2H retention and onboarding figures. The 25% Q4 FY26 flexible-staffing figure is cited to an Intech Group blog. No primary report is reachable.
verdicts.corrected: A staffing-software vendor's page claims GCC contractual roles went from 1 in 5 to 1 in 4 and projects 1 in 3 by FY27, footnoting a 2024 trade article (not the Quess Q4 FY26 report, which it cites only for C2H retention of 15-20% and 40-50% faster onboarding). The 25% Q4 FY26 figure traces to a third-party blog. No primary source is obtainable — do not cite any of this externally.

verdicts.claim: Mainstream enterprise/government IT staffing rate cards have no zero-experience band; Junior already assumes 12-36 months, so a fresher maps to no category a buyer can raise a task order against
verdicts.issue: The bands are right (Junior 12-36, Mid 36-60, Senior 60-84, Expert 84+ months; Junior Developer/Programmer $48.29 Normal / $51.68 High). But the finding omits the footnote directly beneath the table, which defeats its own conclusion: '*Typical Experience is representative of the Skill Level, and has the potential to be adjusted, based on the role being filled. State Agencies will use their best judgment in defining the Skill Level that is most appropriate for their given role when creating a task order.' The date is also wrong — the IFB is dated 1 September 2015 with bids due 5 October 2015, not a cycle beginning 1 September 2016.
verdicts.corrected: North Carolina's IFB ITS-009440 (1 September 2015) defines Junior = 12-36 months, Mid = 36-60, Senior = 60-84, Expert = 84+, with Junior Developer/Programmer at $48.29-$51.68/hr. However, the table's own footnote states experience is 'representative' and 'has the potential to be adjusted, based on the role being filled', with agencies using best judgment per task order. So the rate card discourages a fresher but does not structurally exclude one — the barrier is buyer preference, not a procurement-system impossibility.

verdicts.claim: The remedy buyers write into staffing contracts is unilateral removal plus free replacement, not a refund or guarantee window
verdicts.issue: Both quotes are verbatim, but the finding splices two clauses that do different work. Attachment G 5(b) gives the State the right to disapprove continuing assignment and then says only that if the vendor cannot replace, 'the parties agree to employ best commercial efforts to informally resolve such failure equitably' — no free-replacement guarantee. The 'suitable personnel at no additional cost' language in 5(c) is expressly conditioned on the employee being 'unable to perform due to illness, resignation, or other factors beyond Vendor's control' — i.e. involuntary unavailability, not performance-based removal.
verdicts.corrected: NC IFB §5.2 lets the Agency 'refuse access to or require replacement of any such personnel for cause, including... technical or training qualifications, quality of work', and Attachment G 5(b) reserves the right to 'disapprove the continuing assignment of Vendor personnel'. Free replacement ('suitable personnel at no additional cost') appears separately in 5(c) and is limited to illness, resignation or other causes beyond the vendor's control; where disapproval is for cause and the vendor cannot replace, the contract falls back on 'best commercial efforts to informally resolve such failure equitably'. The directional point stands — buyers write removal rights, not refunds — but 'removal plus free replacement' is not a single contractual package.

verdicts.claim: GeM manpower SLA hardcodes a 2-day replacement SLA and per-day financial penalties
verdicts.issue: Every figure verifies verbatim against the published SLA: non-deployment 1%/day of total value up to 15 days (2%/day at second instance) then cancellation with 10% charges; absence beyond 2 days = substitute within 2 days failing which 1%/day (3%/day second instance) up to 15 days; poor performance = 'Service Provider shall immediately replace'; theft/misconduct = 'Replacement of employee within 2 days'; termination where 'cumulative penalties rise to 10% of the contract value' or 'repeated breach of any SLA beyond 3 instances'.

verdicts.claim: GeM SLA requires a documented per-candidate compliance dossier; false certification is a contractual breach
verdicts.issue: Verbatim: 'The biodata/ resume, qualification and experience of the said manpower should be certified by the Service Provider. In case any of such document is found to be false at any stage, it would be deemed to be a breach of terms of contract making the Service Provider liable for legal action.' Also confirmed: police verification certificate, Aadhaar copy, identity and residence proof at deployment; photo ID card 'within 8 days of joining'; and pre-assessment on 'educational qualification, work experience, skill assessment, pre-interviewing, short-listing'.

verdicts.claim: Statutory-compliance evidence is a hard payment condition: EPF/ESI proof required with bills, deposit by the 15th, Rs 100/200 per day penalties
verdicts.issue: The bill-hold and penalty figures are verbatim ('shall be necessarily accompanied with the documentary proof'; 'A requisite portion of the bill/whole of the bill amount will be held up till such proof is furnished'; Rs. 100 per day first default, Rs. 200 plus payment hold second, then cancellation with 10% charges). But the same document states two different deposit deadlines, and the finding reports only one: clause 4.3 requires employer's share deposited 'within first 7 working days of the succeeding month', while a later clause says 'within 15th day of the month of payment'. Citing only the 15th understates the stricter obligation in the same contract.
verdicts.corrected: Under the GeM SLA, EPF/ESI claims in bills 'shall be necessarily accompanied with the documentary proof' and 'a requisite portion of the bill/whole of the bill amount will be held up till such proof is furnished'. Note the document carries two inconsistent deposit deadlines — proof of deposit 'within first 7 working days of the succeeding month' in one clause and 'within 15th day of the month of payment' in another — so plan to the 7-working-day limit. Delay in take-home pay or PF/ESI deposit attracts Rs 100/day (first instance), Rs 200/day plus payment hold (second), then cancellation with 10% charges. Separately, the next month's bill is paid 'only after submission of certificate of disbursement of wages of previous month'.

verdicts.claim: Buyers measure staffing vendors on submission quality and early attrition, not training quality: ≥75% qualified, <5% fail-to-start/2-week leavers, <5% negative attrition, 95% timesheets
verdicts.issue: NC IFB §6.1 verifies exactly (6.1.1 75%, 6.1.2 <5%, 6.1.3 <5%, 6.1.4 95%), as does §6.2 — root-cause analysis within ten calendar days, State-approved cure plan implemented within ten days, monthly monitoring, removal for continued failure. One omission worth knowing: there is a fifth SLA, 6.1.5 'Total Dollar Value of Supplemental Staffing Assignment' with a target of > $0, reviewed yearly — i.e. the contract also measures whether you win any work at all.

verdicts.claim: Sackett et al.: job experience in years predicts at ρ = .07 vs structured interviews .42, job-knowledge tests .40, work samples .33
verdicts.issue: Table 3 verifies every figure exactly: structured interviews .42, job knowledge .40, empirically keyed biodata .38, work samples .33, cognitive ability .31, integrity .31, assessment centres .29, unstructured interviews .19, job experience (years) .07 against Schmidt & Hunter's .18. One precision point: 'years of education .10' sits in the separate 'excluded for insufficient information' block and is a Schmidt & Hunter 1998 legacy value, not a revised estimate, so it should not be listed alongside the revised column.

verdicts.claim: A structured job tryout is the highest-validity selection device in the legacy evidence base (.44), well above reference checks (.26)
verdicts.issue: The two numbers are right and correctly identified as excluded-for-insufficient-information legacy estimates, but 'highest-validity' is false on the face of the same table. Within the same excluded block, peer ratings are .49 and T&E behavioural consistency method .45 — both above .44. In the Schmidt & Hunter column proper, work sample tests .54, cognitive ability .51, structured interviews .51 and job knowledge tests .48 are all higher. Taking this into a sales conversation as stated is a falsifiable overclaim.
verdicts.corrected: In Sackett et al.'s Table 3, 'job tryout procedure' is listed at .44 and 'reference checks' at .26 among procedures excluded from the revised matrix for insufficient information (both Schmidt & Hunter 1998 / Hunter & Hunter 1984 legacy estimates). A tryout is not the highest-validity device in that evidence base — peer ratings (.49) and T&E behavioural consistency (.45) rank above it in the same block, and work samples (.54), cognitive ability (.51) and structured interviews (.51) rank higher in the legacy column. The usable claim is narrower: a tryout substantially outperforms reference checks, and the ordering supports a paid trial over asking third parties about a candidate.

verdicts.claim: Hands-on trial is the single most influential B2B proof asset and vendors under-supply it
verdicts.issue: All figures verify in the PDF: 40% of buyers used free trials and 74% of those called them the most influential resource; demos used by 54% (67% enterprise) with 71% of users calling them most influential; prior experience 52% and influential for 71%; and verbatim, 'When we asked vendors what their top five marketing tactics were, free trials didn't crack the list.' Sample of 2,164 technology buyers confirmed in the methodology section.

verdicts.claim: 56% of buyers (71% enterprise) talk to an existing customer before buying; vendors underestimate this by ~20 points
verdicts.issue: The 2024 half verifies verbatim — '56% of buyers said they had conversations with a product user before purchasing (71% were for enterprise purchase prices)' and 'Vendors estimate this number is much lower, guessing an average of 34%, with one-quarter of vendors guessing 12% or under' (a 22-point gap). The 2025 edition figures (2,058 buyers, 490 vendors, published 8 April 2025, 54% vs 38% vendor estimate, 77% consulting reviews) were not verified — that source was not fetched.
verdicts.corrected: TrustRadius 2024 (2,164 verified buyers): 56% of buyers had a conversation with a product user before purchasing, 71% at enterprise purchase prices, against a vendor estimate averaging 34% — a 22-point gap, with a quarter of vendors guessing 12% or under. The 2025 ninth-annual figures quoted alongside this are unverified and should be dropped or re-checked before use. The strategic implication stands: with zero referenceable clients, Anvi cannot supply the most-used late-stage validation channel.

verdicts.claim: 51% of buyers want transparent pricing and 47% of enterprise buyers want ROI easier to calculate; 66% chose on best price
verdicts.issue: The 66% figure verifies for all buyers ('It met our needs for the best price: 66% (58% for enterprise purchase prices)'). But 51% and 47% are both taken from a list the report explicitly labels 'Enterprise purchase price top five were:' — so the 51% transparent-pricing figure is an enterprise-buyer number, not an all-buyer number as the finding states.
verdicts.corrected: TrustRadius 2024: among enterprise-purchase-price buyers, 51% said 'I wish all vendors had transparent pricing' and 47% said 'I wish calculating ROI were easier so I could get the budget approved' (both from the enterprise top-five list, not the all-buyer figures). Separately, across all buyers, 66% chose the product they bought because 'It met our needs for the best price' (58% at enterprise). Anvi publishes neither price bands nor an ROI comparison.

verdicts.claim: Analyst-report usage has fallen to a seven-year low of 16%, making bought analyst validation a low-yield trust play
verdicts.issue: Verbatim from the report: 'the use of analyst reports reaches historically low usage at 16%—the lowest it has been in seven years and continuing to trend down', alongside user-review usage staying flat over the same seven years. Note the report also shows Gartner is the 5th-most-used research website for enterprise buyers at 27%, so analyst brands retain some top-of-funnel presence even as report consumption falls.

verdicts.claim: Hinge: fewer than 60% of buyers now ask for referrals (a 15% decrease); ~60% rate their vendor highly on reputation but only ~23% consider it well known
verdicts.issue: Not checked — the source page was not fetched within this session's budget. It is also a marketing firm's own research summary with no stated edition date (the finding itself concedes 'edition dates not stated on the summary page'), so even once fetched it will not support a dated, auditable claim. Do not put the '15% decrease' figure in any investor or client material without the underlying report.

verdicts.claim: CV-validation discrepancies run at 12.80% in Indian IT, making an unqualified 'pre-screened bench' claim a liability
verdicts.issue: Every percentage matches the cited article: overall white-collar 4.33%, gig 5.61%, IT CV-validation 12.80%, employment history 11.15%, address 7.68%, education 4.49%, reference checks 4.17%, for H1 FY2026. Two cautions: this is trade press reporting a background-verification vendor's own commercial dataset with no published methodology, and the finding's gloss that 'roughly one submitted profile in eight contains a material inaccuracy' generalises an IT-sector CV-validation sub-metric into an all-profile claim. Use it as a buyer-objection you must pre-empt, not as a statistic you assert.

verdicts.claim: Gartner projects 1 in 4 candidate profiles worldwide will be fake by 2028; 6% of candidates admitted interview fraud; 38.5% of 19,368 interviews showed AI-cheating behaviour
verdicts.issue: The finding itself concedes Gartner's own release was not retrieved, and the only source is a staffing-industry blog. The 38.5%/19,368-interview analysis is vendor-run 'trade analysis' with no published methodology. A prediction attributed to a paywalled analyst house through a trade blog cannot be put in front of a procurement team — they can check it and you cannot.

verdicts.claim: Indian IT fresher intake fell from ~600,000 (FY22) to ~250,000 (FY23); top-five net headcount -70,000 FY24 and +9,500 FY25; TCS bench tolerance now 30-45 days vs 80-90
verdicts.issue: Not fetched within budget. All of it rests on a single news article quoting one executive (TeamLease Digital's CEO) rather than a published dataset, and the TCS 225-billable-days and 30-45-day figures are reported internal policy. The directional argument — that bench economics are tightening — is almost certainly sound, but these specific numbers are not independently verified and should not be quoted as facts.

verdicts.claim: 74%+ of Indian employers planned to hire freshers for AI roles (TeamLease) while ~55% of Indian IT firms recorded lower entry-level hiring and entry-level share fell 28%→15% (Nomura)
verdicts.issue: Neither source was fetched. Both legs are survey/analyst material reaching us through secondary channels (IBEF summarising a vendor's survey; Nomura via trade press). The underlying point — that stated intent and observed requisitions diverge — is the right caution for Anvi's messaging, but neither number is verified.

verdicts.claim: Revature's Emerging Talent Program publishes zero upfront cost, <5% performance attrition, 70% faster productivity, 40-55% lower year-one TCO, 3-10 week training, 200+ hours free prep, 0-24 month coaching, and one anonymised case
verdicts.issue: The programme page verifies all of it: 'Zero upfront cost with FTE conversion', 'Conversion option with zero-obligation timing', '<5% performance-related attrition with mentoring', '70% faster time-to-productivity', '40–55% lower total cost of ownership vs. traditional delivery models (year one)', '3–10 Weeks' client-specific training, '200+ Hours of free prep', 'Mentor & Elevate (0–24 Months)', and the GenAI healthcare case at 50% increase in use-case identification and 40% reduction in AI hiring costs. The case study also carries a 4.8/5 participant satisfaction score the finding omits. Homepage-level counts and awards were not verified from this URL.

verdicts.claim: Large accounts carry a managed-service tax: 4.0% administrative fee plus 1.96% MSP vendor fee, both inside not-to-exceed rates, so $90.00 bills at $95.36
verdicts.issue: Verbatim from §5.5-5.6, including the worked example: 'Vendor Hourly Rate: $90.00 per hour (includes all Vendor costs) / OITS Administrative Fee: 4.00% / MSP Vendor Fee: 1.96% / Adjusted MSP bill to the State: $95.36 per hour.' The rate-card headers confirm 'IT ADMIN Fee & MSP Fee INCLUDED' in the NTE rates. The ~6% off the top before funding any guarantee is correct — though note this is a 2015 US state programme, so treat it as a structural illustration of VMS/MSP economics rather than an Indian or current benchmark.

verdicts.claim: NYSERDA RFP 3525 requires proposers to 'identify conditions, timelines and fees associated with converting a resource', so an undefined contract-to-hire path is a disqualifier
verdicts.issue: Not fetched. The finding already concedes the document date is unconfirmed and that the URL was found via a search index. A single US state-authority RFP would in any case be weak support for the strong claim that buyers 'formally require' this — and it says nothing about Indian buyer practice. The underlying advice (publish conversion conditions, timeline and fee basis) is sound on its own merits without this citation.

verdicts.claim: India's four labour codes came into force on 21 November 2025, raising compliance proof demands and bench-carrying cost
verdicts.issue: No government source confirms this within this session. labour.gov.in, PIB, indiacode.nic.in and epfo.gov.in all refused or returned no usable content, and the finding's own sources are a legal directory and law-firm alerts. Separately, a cached law-firm guide corroborates the date and adds a fact every one of these labour-code findings omits: a corrigendum dated 19 December 2025 modified the 21 November notification so that the EPF Act 1952 was repealed in its entirety, creating a live 'basic wages' vs 'wages' computation ambiguity. Per the official-source test this is unverifiable; commission written legal advice before pricing anything on it.

verdicts.claim: The addressable comparison set is a ~USD 5.6bn Indian IT flexi-staffing market of ~663,000 workers
verdicts.issue: The core numbers verify in the cited article: 'The Indian IT flexi staffing market was worth $4.9 billion (around Rs 40,580 crore) in the financial year ended March 2024, employing 5.97 lakh people' and 'By the end of the financial year ending March 2026, it is expected to be worth $5.6 billion, with a workforce of 6.63 lakh.' But the article contains nothing about 9.16 million by FY27 or 7.2 million in FY25 — those are attributed to a different source and do not belong in a claim cited to this URL. Note too that the USD 5.6bn/663,000 figure is a November 2024 projection for FY26, and FY26 has now closed, so it should be refreshed against actuals.
verdicts.corrected: Indian Staffing Federation data reported in November 2024 put Indian IT flexi staffing at USD 4.9bn (about Rs 40,580 crore) employing 597,000 people in the year ended March 2024, projected to reach about USD 5.6bn and 663,000 workers by the year ended March 2026. The wider 9.16m-by-FY27 and 7.2m-FY25 flexi-workforce figures are not in this source and must be cited separately. Because FY26 has now closed, replace the projection with an actual before publishing. The substantive point holds: this, not the AI training-dataset market, is Anvi's comparison set.

verdicts.claim: CLRA 1970 and its 1971 Central Rules were repealed into the OSH Code 2020 on 21 November 2025, so any 'CLRA licence' reference on the site is out of date
verdicts.issue: No official source confirms the repeal within this session; the cited source is a law-firm knowledge portal. A cached law-firm guide does state the 29 central laws subsumed by the Codes 'stand repealed' as of 21 November 2025, which supports the direction. The practical instruction — stop citing 'CLRA licence' as the governing instrument until counsel confirms the current one — is prudent regardless, since citing a repealed statute is a credibility risk either way.

verdicts.claim: The contract-labour licensing threshold doubled from 20 to 50 workers, so no contractor licence is needed below 50 deployed contract workers
verdicts.issue: Not confirmed by any government source. A cached law-firm guide corroborates 'a single unified threshold of 50 or more contract labour for applicability of contract labour related provisions – both in respect of a principal employer and a contractor', which the finding does not mention — the threshold applies on both sides. Treating a 50-worker safe harbour as a 12-24 month runway on the strength of law-firm commentary is exactly the kind of decision that needs a written opinion, because the finding's own corollary is that the 50th deployment turns an unlicensed supply into an offence.

verdicts.claim: 'Contractor' under the OSH Code now expressly includes a person who supplies manpower as a mere human resource, closing the argument that pure bench-deployment is outside the contract-labour regime
verdicts.issue: This is the most consequential error in the set, and it points the wrong way. A cached law-firm guide states that the OSH Code narrowed, not widened, the exposure for a model like Anvi's: 'While judicial guidance and nation-wide practices under the previous regime excluded service provision arrangements from the ambit of the CLRA, this principle is now specifically codified under the OSH Code, by excluding personnel who are regularly employed by, and are paid wages and provided benefits by, the contractor, from the ambit of contract labour.' Anvi's engineers are on Anvi's payroll receiving wages and statutory benefits — which is precisely the codified exclusion. The finding asserts the argument is 'closed' when the Code appears to have opened it.
verdicts.corrected: The OSH Code's contractor definition does cover supply of manpower, but the Code also codifies an exclusion from 'contract labour' for personnel who are regularly employed by, and paid wages and provided benefits by, the contractor. Because Anvi's engineers sit on Anvi's payroll with statutory benefits, Anvi may fall within that exclusion rather than inside the contract-labour regime — the opposite of the finding's conclusion. This is the single highest-value question to put to counsel, since it also governs the s.57 core-activity exposure below.

verdicts.claim: Section 57 of the OSH Code prohibits contract labour in a client's core activity, the single largest legal threat to deploying engineers into client engineering teams
verdicts.issue: The prohibition and its three exceptions are corroborated by a cached law-firm guide, which confirms the ban is now nationwide ('previously restricted in limited States like Telangana and Andhra Pradesh only') and that whether an activity is core 'is left to the designated authorities'. Two corrections. First, no government source was reachable, so the statutory text is unverified. Second, and materially, the finding's severity rating does not survive the point above: if Anvi's engineers are regularly employed and paid benefits by Anvi, they are excluded from 'contract labour' altogether and s.57 does not reach them. The threat is contingent on a classification question the finding treats as settled against Anvi.
verdicts.corrected: Law-firm commentary indicates the OSH Code prohibits engaging contract labour in a principal employer's core activity nationwide, subject to three exceptions (activity ordinarily done through a contractor; not requiring full-time workers for the major portion of hours; sudden increase in volume), with classification left to designated authorities. For a software client, engineering is core. But this exposure only bites if Anvi's engineers are 'contract labour' — and the Code excludes personnel regularly employed by and paid wages and benefits by the contractor. Resolve the classification question first; the s.57 risk is conditional on it, not the standalone largest threat.

verdicts.claim: Central rules were notified 8 May 2026 as OSH (Central) Rules 2026 via G.S.R. 345(E), with Shram Suvidha as the single registration and licensing portal and 5-year contractor licences
verdicts.issue: No government source reachable; the cited sources are a boutique firm's blog post and a Big Four flash alert, and the blog's own URL says 'notified by Ministry on May 9' while the claim says 8 May — the citation contradicts the date it is offered to support. A cached law-firm guide does corroborate that the OSH Code allows a 'work-specific license' for project-based work orders and a 'national license' for multi-state work, and the concept of deemed approval on timeline lapse. The gazette number and date must be confirmed against the e-Gazette before anything is built on it.

verdicts.claim: Contractor licensing economics are modest: INR 1,000 security deposit per contract labour, 5-year validity, renewal 90-30 days before expiry with 25% late fee
verdicts.issue: Sourced only to a tax-blog analysis of rules this session could not reach officially. Every figure here — deposit per worker, the crore-level caps, renewal window, 25% uplift, 7-day renewal obligation, Form XXI and Form XVII references — is the kind of detail that moves between draft and final rules. The conclusion ('for a 100-person bench the deposit is roughly INR 1 lakh — so there is no cost excuse for operating unlicensed past 50') is sound reasoning but rests entirely on unverified inputs.

verdicts.claim: Telangana has not yet finalised its state rules under three of the four Codes — all still at draft stage as of late 2026
verdicts.issue: The substance is confirmed by an official source, but the count is wrong. The Telangana Labour Department's own site carries a live banner reading: 'All Stake Holders are requested to furnish their opinion on the four(4) draft State Labour Rules on Labour Codes... The last date for furnishing of opinion is 15-06-2026.' So it is all four Codes at draft stage, not three — the Code on Wages rules are in draft too, which matters because another finding asserts Telangana is 'already enforcing' that Code. The banner is still displayed in October 2026, which does corroborate that none has been finalised.
verdicts.corrected: Telangana has not finalised its state rules under ANY of the four Labour Codes. The Telangana Labour Department's site shows all four draft State Labour Rules out for stakeholder comment with a closing date of 15 June 2026, and the notice remains posted as of 7 October 2026. For a staffing firm whose appropriate government is the State, this is a genuinely ambiguous transition period governed by the Codes' repeal-and-savings clauses — which is why Anvi should take written legal advice rather than rely on a compliance vendor's checklist.

verdicts.claim: Telangana G.O.Ms.No.6 dated 30 May 2026 fixed new minimum wages effective 1 June 2026, Zone-I highly-skilled at INR 20,000 basic
verdicts.issue: Not confirmed. The Telangana Labour Department's acts-and-rules and minimum-wages pages are session-gated and returned no content, and the cited sources are compliance vendors. There is also tension with the finding above: the same department still has its draft Code on Wages rules out for comment, so 'already enforcing the Code on Wages' needs care. The commercial conclusion — that undeployed bench staff on Anvi's payroll must still be paid at least the rate for their classification plus VDA, setting a hard floor on bench cost — is the right thing to model, but confirm the G.O. number, date and zone figures with counsel before pricing.

verdicts.claim: Telangana Shops and Establishments registration is due within 30 days, expires 31 December of the year of issue, fees INR 100 to INR 10,000+ by headcount
verdicts.issue: Sourced to an HR-software compliance page and a company-secretarial vendor, with no official confirmation obtained. Fee slabs and renewal mechanics are precisely the details these aggregators get stale, and an annual certificate expiring on 31 December regardless of issue date is an unusual rule worth confirming directly with the Department before relying on it for a registration calendar.

verdicts.claim: Telangana's IT/ITeS exemption from working-hours provisions has been extended to 29 May 2028, conditional on a 48-hour week, overtime beyond 48 hours and a weekly day off
verdicts.issue: Single trade-alert source; no government notification obtained. The structural caution the finding draws is the valuable part and does not depend on the exact expiry date: an exemption from specified sections is not an exemption from the Act, so registration, records, leave and wage obligations continue. If Anvi markets client-timezone or flexible shifts, confirm the current conditions directly — the 48-hour cap and overtime liability are the binding constraints and an expired or amended exemption would be an unpleasant discovery.

verdicts.claim: Telangana professional tax: nil to INR 15,000, INR 150 for 15,001-20,000, INR 200 above 20,000, PTRC returns and payment by the 10th
verdicts.issue: Cited to a calculator blog. The official Telangana Commercial Taxes site was displaying an emergency-maintenance notice when checked, so the PT Act, Rules and schedule pages could not be read. The amounts are small and the finding's own point is that the exposure is roughly INR 200 per deployed head per month; the real risk it identifies is the recurring monthly filing, which is worth confirming from the Department's own PT schedule rather than a third-party page.

verdicts.claim: EPF applies at 20 employees and the INR 15,000 wage ceiling was deliberately retained by a notification dated 29 May 2026 despite a Supreme Court order of 5 January 2026
verdicts.issue: epfo.gov.in could not be read (redirect then 404) and no gazette notification was obtained; the sources are a trade alert and a legal database. This is a compound claim — a judicial direction, a four-month window, and a deliberate decision not to revise — and each element needs separate verification. The finding's own caveat is the operative advice and survives the verification failure: do not price client contracts on the assumption that an INR 1,800 monthly PF cap is permanent.

verdicts.claim: The Employees' Provident Funds Scheme 2026, notified 29 June 2026, caps mandatory PF at INR 1,800/month with everything above voluntary and no employer duty to match
verdicts.issue: No official source; cited to a law firm and a business daily. This claim is also in tension with a fact none of these findings carries: a cached law-firm guide records that a corrigendum of 19 December 2025 repealed the EPF Act 1952 in its entirety, leaving the 1952 Scheme operating under s.164(2)(b) of the Social Security Code and creating ambiguity over whether contributions compute on 'basic wages' or the Code's wider 'wages'. Treating a INR 1,800 cap as a settled margin lever while that ambiguity is open is risky, and it interacts with the 50%-wage-rule claim below.

verdicts.claim: A new joiner above INR 15,000/month who was never previously an EPF member can be treated as an excluded employee, but anyone with a prior UAN must be enrolled regardless of salary
verdicts.issue: Sourced to a payroll vendor's academy page and an HR community forum — the weakest sourcing in the regulatory set, for a rule that directly determines statutory cost per head. The distinction drawn is the standard market understanding and the cohort insight is genuinely useful (first-job trainees vs career-switchers carry different statutory cost structures), but a payroll-vendor help page is not a basis for a cost model. Confirm from the Scheme text.

verdicts.claim: ESI registration triggers at 10 employees, ceiling INR 21,000 gross (INR 25,000 for persons with disability), rates employer 3.25% and employee 0.75% unchanged since July 2019
verdicts.issue: The rates are confirmed by the official source. esic.gov.in states: 'Currently, the employee's contribution rate (w.e.f. 01.07.2019) is 0.75% of the wages and that of employer's is 3.25% of the wages paid/payable.' The same page adds a detail the finding omits and which matters for stipend-paying trainees: employees on a daily average wage up to Rs.176 are exempt from their own contribution while the employer still pays its share. The 10-employee trigger and the INR 21,000/25,000 ceilings were not confirmed on the official page and remain unverified.
verdicts.corrected: ESI contribution rates are officially confirmed at employer 3.25% and employee 0.75% with effect from 1 July 2019, and employees on a daily average wage up to Rs.176 are exempt from the employee share while the employer still contributes. Contributions are payable within 15 days of the last day of the calendar month. The 10-employee registration trigger and the INR 21,000 gross ceiling (INR 25,000 for persons with disability) are widely reported but were not confirmed against an official source — verify before modelling. The practical point stands: ESI bites mainly on trainees, stipended bench staff and internal support roles.

verdicts.claim: Gratuity liability for fixed-term staffing now starts at one year, not five — roughly 4.8% of wages per year accruing from month 12
verdicts.issue: Cited to a tax-news site and a law firm; no official confirmation obtained. This is flagged as 'the biggest unmodelled cost change for a contract-staffing P&L', and it is being asserted on secondary sources while also depending on the unverified 50%-wage-rule claim below for its base. If both are right the compounding is real and material; if either is wrong the bill-rate model is wrong. This pair should be the first item in a scoped legal opinion, not absorbed from commentary.

verdicts.claim: The Code on Wages 50% rule: excluded allowances cannot exceed 50% of total remuneration and any excess is added back to 'wages' for PF, gratuity and bonus
verdicts.issue: No official source; cited to a single law firm. This is the mechanism that makes the gratuity change above expensive, so the two must be verified together. A cached law-firm guide independently flags a related live ambiguity — that the schemes refer to 'basic wages' while the Social Security Code requires contributions on 'wages', and that employers 'may face some ambiguity and implementation hurdles during this transition period'. The directional conclusion is safe to plan on: the thin-basic-plus-large-special-allowance structure can no longer be assumed to reduce statutory cost.

verdicts.claim: Written appointment letters are now mandatory for every employee including fixed-term and part-time, with penalties to INR 2,00,000 first offence and INR 3,00,000 plus INR 2,000/day for repeats
verdicts.issue: Cited to a calculator blog and a Big Four alert, with no official confirmation. The specific penalty amounts and the reported 20 February 2026 issue-by date for existing employees are precisely the figures to confirm from the Rules. That said, the operational advice needs no statutory citation to be worth acting on: a hire-train-deploy business moving people from trainee to bench to deployment should document every status change, because a missing appointment letter is the first thing a client's vendor audit finds.

verdicts.claim: The client, as principal employer, carries statutory back-stop liability for Anvi's PF defaults and unpaid wages
verdicts.issue: The cited CGIT appellate order was not fetched and the OSH Rules element rests on a tax-blog analysis. A cached law-firm guide does corroborate and in fact strengthens the direction: it records that the OSH Code departs from CLRA by making contract-labour welfare obligations 'the primary responsibility of the principal employer', with no statutory route to recoup costs, and that liability attaches to the principal employer where a contractor is not duly licensed. So the commercial conclusion is well supported even though the legal citations are not verified: a procurement team is being asked to absorb real risk, and a site with no registration numbers, compliance disclosures or indemnity position gives them no reason to.

verdicts.claim: GST at 18% applies to the gross invoice including salaries and statutory dues under SAC 998513/998514, so a 10% gross-margin deal carries GST ~1.8x the margin
verdicts.issue: The substantive holding is confirmed from an official source, but not the one cited. The Telangana AAR order the finding references for this point (Sri Bhavani Developers, TSAAR 38/2022) was not verified. What is verified, from the GST Council's own published order, is TSAAR 14/2021 (A.R.Com/03/2019, dated 8 October 2021): 'The applicant is not a pure agent under GST Law. Further the deductions available under Section 15 of the CGST Act do not include the amounts pertaining to EPF, ESI, Salary, or Wages. Therefore entire amount received from the Hospital are exigible to CGST / SGST Act 2017.' The 18% rate itself and the SAC assignments were not confirmed officially.
verdicts.corrected: The gross-value principle is confirmed by an official source: Telangana AAR order TSAAR No. 14/2021 dated 8 October 2021 held that a manpower supplier 'is not a pure agent under GST Law', that Section 15 deductions 'do not include the amounts pertaining to EPF, ESI, Salary, or Wages', and that the 'entire amount received' is taxable. The 18% rate, the SAC 998513/998514 codes, the absence of reverse charge on general manpower and recipient ITC eligibility were not verified against official sources and should be confirmed with a GST adviser. The working-capital consequence is the real finding: Anvi funds payroll monthly and remits GST on the full invoice while clients pay on 30-60 day terms.

verdicts.claim: Finance Act 2026 brought supply of manpower within the definition of 'work' for TDS, fixing the rate at 1-2% from 1 April 2026
verdicts.issue: Cited to two consultancy analyses; no Finance Act text, CBDT circular or official confirmation obtained. This claim is characterised as 'cash-flow positive', which makes it exactly the sort of favourable assumption worth verifying before it enters a model — if it is wrong and clients withhold at 10% of gross, the finding's own arithmetic shows the deduction exceeds a thin staffing margin. The correct handling of the deduction (a receivable, not a cost) is right either way.

verdicts.claim: A central placement-agency licensing regime is being drafted and Maharashtra already criminalises unregistered operation with up to three years' imprisonment
verdicts.issue: No official source for either the draft Bill or Maharashtra Act 24 of 2025; cited to an employment-law network and a law firm. Note the finding's most useful conclusions are negative ones — 'There is currently no central licence for domestic placement' and 'Telangana has no equivalent statute that this research could identify' — and absence findings from secondary sources are inherently weak evidence. Track this; do not plan around it.

verdicts.claim: Training bonds are enforceable only up to documented, provable training cost; a round-number bond would be read down as an unenforceable penalty
verdicts.issue: Not fetched. Because Anvi's whole model is funded by training freshers before deployment, bond design is a core commercial document and this is the wrong claim to take from an unfetched law-firm newsletter. The drafting instruction is nonetheless the right default: cost the recovery figure from documented spend per candidate (trainer hours, compute, assessment, stipend) rather than setting a deterrent round number, because that survives scrutiny under either reading.

verdicts.claim: NAPS reimburses 25% of the prescribed stipend up to INR 1,500 per apprentice per month via DBT, and apprentices are not 'workers' for most labour-law purposes
verdicts.issue: Cited to a policy think-tank, not MSDE or the apprenticeship portal. This one is worth properly verifying rather than dropping, because it is the only finding in the set that identifies money flowing toward Anvi rather than away: a direct subsidy for exactly the pre-deployment training stage Anvi funds out of pocket. The claim that apprentices fall outside most labour-law obligations would also change the compliance profile of the training phase, and that is a significant enough consequence to need an official basis.

verdicts.claim: POSH obligations attach at 10 or more workers and extend to staffing-agency personnel at client premises
verdicts.issue: Sourced to a compliance-training vendor's blog. The 10-worker Internal Committee threshold and composition requirements are long-standing and very likely correct, but an unverified vendor blog is thin support for a claim about statutory exposure. The gap identified is real and specific to Anvi's model — cohort-based training programmes and client-site deployments both sit inside this exposure, and a policy that does not expressly cover contract workers and agency personnel leaves it uncovered. Verify from the Act and confirm the Local Committee fallback position.

verdicts.claim: The correct market statistic is the formal flexi-staffing market at ~INR 2,20,000 crore in FY26 with a workforce going from 7.2 million (FY25) to 9.16 million (FY27)
verdicts.issue: This recommendation substantially overstates its cited source, which is serious because it is the number Anvi is being told to put on its website. The DT Next article supports only three things: 9.7% YoY growth in FY25, 1.39 lakh new formal flexi workers added, and ISF members' flexi workforce at 1.8 million as of March 2025 — not 1.83 million at end-June 2025. The article contains nothing about INR 2,20,000 crore for FY26, nothing about 9.16 million by FY27 or 7.2 million in FY25, and nothing about growth slowing to 6.1%. The Grand View Research critique is separately verified and correct.
verdicts.corrected: Indian Staffing Federation data reported in July 2025 confirms the formal flexi-staffing industry grew 9.7% YoY in FY25, adding 1.39 lakh new formal flexi workers, with ISF members' flexi workforce at 1.8 million as of March 2025. The INR 2,20,000 crore FY26 estimate, the 7.2m-to-9.16m FY25-FY27 workforce projection and the 6.1% slowdown are NOT in this source — source them properly or drop them before publishing. The Grand View Research point is verified and stands: its USD 8.60bn figure measures the AI training-dataset market, not talent demand, and citing it signals the vendor has not sized its own market.

verdicts.claim: Contract staffing and manpower supply attract 18% GST with full ITC under the SAC 9985 family (998511-998515)
verdicts.issue: Cited to a GST software vendor's SAC reference page — not an official rate notification or the CBIC tariff. The SAC sub-code breakdown and the 18% rate are the market's standard understanding, and the invoice-hygiene advice (show headcount, days/hours and SAC on the invoice face; use 998513 when the engineer stays on Anvi's rolls versus 998511/998512 for one-time placement fees) is sensible operationally. But the rate and classification that determine every invoice Anvi raises should be confirmed against CBIC, not a vendor page.

verdicts.claim: The 22 September 2025 GST rate rationalisation collapsed slabs to 5/18/40 but left staffing at 18%
verdicts.issue: No CBIC notification obtained; cited to a Big Four alert and a software vendor. The practical instruction is the valuable part and is safe regardless: do not price on any assumption of a future rate cut for staffing. If a rate change is being relied on in either direction, confirm the notification numbers directly with CBIC.

verdicts.claim: GST is payable on the entire invoice value of a manpower supply including salary and employer EPF/ESI; staffing firms are not 'pure agents'
verdicts.issue: Confirmed from the official GST Council publication of Telangana AAR order TSAAR No. 14/2021 (A.R.Com/03/2019, dated 8 October 2021). The applicant supplied manpower to a hospital and argued it was a pure agent; the Authority held 'The applicant is not a pure agent under GST Law', that 'the deductions available under Section 15 of the CGST Act do not include the amounts pertaining to EPF, ESI, Salary, or Wages', and that the 'entire amount received from the Hospital are exigible to CGST / SGST'. Two refinements: the order reasons under Section 15 generally rather than 15(2) specifically and does not cite Rule 33 by number; and the West Bengal line of rulings was not verified. Note the fact pattern is precisely Anvi's exposure case — a hospital recipient with blocked or no credit bears the tax as a real cost.

verdicts.claim: There is no reverse charge on general manpower supply; RCM applies only to security personnel supplied by a non-body-corporate
verdicts.issue: Cited to a newspaper article and a legal-content site summarising Notification 29/2018-CT(R) — no official notification obtained. Both operational conclusions are commercially significant and should be confirmed with a GST adviser rather than acted on from these sources: that Anvi as a company always charges under forward charge (so a client asserting 'we'll pay under RCM' is wrong), and that sourcing security-adjacent manpower from a proprietorship or partnership would make Anvi liable to self-assess RCM without being able to net it off the sub-vendor invoice.

verdicts.claim: For domestic B2B staffing the place of supply is the client's registered location under Section 12(2) IGST, so Hyderabad-based Anvi charges IGST out-of-state and CGST+SGST in Telangana
verdicts.issue: The finding's own source attribution is candid that this is the 'general position as summarised in export-of-services guides' rather than a verified reading of the statute, and the cited URL is a tax-firm guide about something else entirely. The operational risk it flags is real and worth engineering around: if a Bengaluru client's PO is raised by its Hyderabad branch GSTIN while the engineer works in Bengaluru, following the engineer rather than the GSTIN produces a wrong-tax-head demand with interest and a refund cycle. The actionable fix needs no citation — Anvi's hiring-request form captures no GSTIN or billing-state field, and it should.

verdicts.claim: Deploying engineers at a client's premises in another state does not by itself create a fixed establishment requiring GST registration there
verdicts.issue: The Odisha AAAR order was not obtained; cited to two tax-news aggregators. The finding is commendably honest about the limits of its own conclusion — AAR and AAAR rulings bind only the applicant, and it notes at least one AAR has gone the other way where a site office existed. Since it also identifies this as 'the single biggest cost question in Anvi's model', because multi-state registration means separate GSTINs, returns and ITC pools, it deserves a written opinion and a documented planning position rather than reliance on an unverified ruling summary.

verdicts.claim: Finance Act 2026 omitted Section 13(8)(b) of the IGST Act with effect from 30 March 2026, enabling zero-rated treatment of offshore staffing revenue
verdicts.issue: No official source for the omission, the assent date or the effective date; cited to three advisory firms. This matters more than most because it underpins an export-revenue strategy. The one element that is safe is the structural reasoning the finding offers independently of the amendment: a US or Gulf client contracting for a deployed engineer is a principal-to-principal supply and not intermediary services at all, so with an LUT and FIRC-backed forex receipts it would be zero-rated regardless of how s.13(8)(b) was resolved. Build on that, and confirm the amendment before relying on it.

verdicts.claim: E-invoicing becomes mandatory once aggregate annual turnover crosses INR 5 crore, per CBIC Notification 10/2023 effective 1 August 2023
verdicts.issue: Cited to two CA-community sites rather than CBIC. The threshold is well established in the market, but the consequence the finding identifies deserves emphasis and is independent of the citation: on a staffing P&L the turnover test applies to gross billing including pass-through salary, not margin, so a bench of roughly 25-30 engineers billed at INR 1.5-2 lakh/month breaches INR 5 crore within the first full year. An invoice that should have carried an IRN but did not is an invalid document, letting the client deny ITC and dispute payment — so confirm the threshold and build IRN generation in from the first invoice, not at the point of breach.

verdicts.claim: Government, local authority, PSU and notified clients withhold 2% GST TDS under Section 51 CGST on contracts above INR 2.5 lakh
verdicts.issue: Cited to a compliance software vendor and state study material, not CBIC. The cash-flow analysis is the useful content and is consistent with the public-sector procurement evidence verified elsewhere in this set: 2% of gross billing is locked until the deductor files GSTR-7, public-sector clients are the slowest filers, and the INR 2.5 lakh test applies to the contract rather than the invoice so almost every government staffing contract is caught. Combined with the reverse-auction L1 pricing and the 2-year panel cycles verified below, this reinforces that public-sector work is a poor first market for a bench-funded model.

verdicts.claim: Client income-tax TDS turns on contract (2%) versus professional/technical services (10% or 2%) characterisation, consolidated into Section 393 from 1 April 2026
verdicts.issue: Cited to a business-intelligence site and tax summaries, not CBDT. The old s.194C and s.194J rates and thresholds described are the long-standing position, but the s.393 consolidation and its carry-over of rates needs official confirmation, and it sits in tension with the separate claim above that Finance Act 2026 expressly placed manpower supply inside the s.194C equivalent. The live risk identified is genuine and worth pre-empting contractually: a client treating an 'Applied AI consultant' deployment as professional services and withholding 10% of gross billing would withhold more than the entire margin, recoverable only on assessment a year later.

verdicts.claim: All four Labour Codes came into force 21 November 2025, the contract-labour threshold rose 20 to 50, and a single pan-India contractor licence replaces state-by-state licences
verdicts.issue: No government source; cited to a law firm's snapshot. A cached law-firm guide corroborates the date, the unified 50-or-more threshold applying to both principal employer and contractor, and the availability of a 'national license' for multi-state work plus a 'work-specific license' for project-based orders. But the finding's framing that this is 'genuinely favourable to Anvi' is one-sided: the same guide records that the implementing notifications provide no transitional period, that welfare obligations become the principal employer's primary responsibility with no statutory recoupment, and that liability attaches to the principal employer where the contractor is unlicensed. Treat the licensing simplification as real and the net effect as unsettled.

verdicts.claim: Vijaya Bank v. Prashant B. Narnaware (2025 INSC 691, 14 May 2025) upheld a minimum-service clause with INR 2,00,000 liquidated damages
verdicts.issue: The judgment was not fetched; cited to two law firms and a legal news site. This duplicates an earlier training-bond finding and should be consolidated with it. Note the two findings characterise the same case slightly differently — one says the INR 2,00,000 sum was held 'neither excessive nor punitive' given seniority and operational disruption, the other that the Court 'stressed that the sum must be reasonable and proportionate and must reflect actual recoverable costs'. Those pull in different directions on how much latitude Anvi has, which is precisely why the judgment itself should be read before trainee agreements are drafted.

verdicts.claim: Non-solicitation of employees is enforceable in India; post-employment non-compete against the engineer is not, so Anvi's protection must sit in the client MSA
verdicts.issue: Cited to a case-law aggregator, a legal blog and a working paper; no judgment text verified. The Section 27 position on post-employment non-competes is settled law and uncontroversial, and the Wipro v. Beckman Coulter line on non-solicitation is widely relied on, but none of it was confirmed here. This duplicates a later finding making the same point — consolidate them. The commercial conclusion is the right design principle and does not depend on the citations: an engineer Anvi cannot restrain from joining the client is an engineer Anvi can charge the client a priced conversion fee for.

verdicts.claim: DPDP Rules 2025 were notified 13-14 November 2025 and commence in three tranches, with substantive obligations switching on in May 2027
verdicts.issue: No official source; cited to two law firms and a legal database. The finding's own framing is the part that matters and needs no verification: whatever the exact commencement dates, the design decisions being made now — what consent text sits on the resume-upload form, where resumes live, how long they are kept — are expensive to retrofit once a few thousand candidates are in the database. Treat the runway as shorter than the headline date implies and verify the tranche dates before relying on them for sequencing.

verdicts.claim: Section 7(i) 'employment purposes' does not reliably cover job candidates, so Anvi needs express consent for every resume it collects, screens, verifies and forwards
verdicts.issue: Cited to a law firm and two background-verification vendors — note that BGV vendors have a commercial interest in how strictly these obligations are read. No official source or regulatory guidance obtained, and the finding concedes the position for a not-yet-hired individual is 'unsettled'. The structural observation is sound and specific to Anvi regardless: its entire funnel consists of people who are not its employees, and forwarding a CV to a client is a third-party disclosure. Designing for express, purpose-specific consent and a standalone notice is the conservative default and costs little now.

verdicts.claim: DPDP Rule 7 requires notifying affected individuals without delay, intimating the Board immediately and filing a detailed report within 72 hours, with no materiality threshold
verdicts.issue: Cited to a compliance platform, a vendor brief and industry guidance rather than the Rules. The absence of a materiality threshold or harm test is a strong claim with a sharp consequence — that a misdirected spreadsheet of candidate CVs is a reportable breach — and absence claims from secondary sources are weak. The Rule 6 safeguards described (encryption or tokenisation, access control, logging, backup, one-year log retention) are reasonable security practice to implement irrespective of whether the deadlines are exactly as stated.

verdicts.claim: Section 8(2) requires a written contract with any background-verification vendor or sub-processor, with Rule 6(1)(f) binding processors to prescribed safeguards
verdicts.issue: Cited to three advisory firms, no official source. The genuinely useful analysis here needs no statutory verification: Anvi sits on both sides of the relationship — data fiduciary for candidate data it collects, and processor or joint fiduciary for client data its deployed engineers touch inside client systems. That means two paper trails, a downstream DPA with every BGV vendor, assessment platform and ATS, and an upstream data-processing schedule in the client MSA covering what a deployed engineer may access, log and take with them. Build both; confirm the specific clause list with counsel.

verdicts.claim: If Anvi charges candidates for training, that fee carries 18% GST — no educational-institution exemption for commercial training and coaching
verdicts.issue: Cited to a tax-filing site and a state FAQ PDF; the individual AAR rulings were not verified.
